name: Levomilnacipran (Fetzima)
summary: Once-daily SNRI for major depression. Often felt as more “get-up-and-go” than sedating, but nausea, sweating, sexual side effects, and blood pressure/heart rate bumps can show up—especially early.
description: Fetzima is an SNRI antidepressant used for major depressive disorder (MDD). It’s taken once daily as an extended-release capsule that you swallow whole. Some people notice early shifts in energy and focus within 1–2 weeks, with fuller mood improvement building over 4–6 weeks. Biggest watch-outs: the antidepressant suicidality warning in people 24 and under, serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic meds, blood pressure/heart rate increases, urinary hesitancy/retention, hyponatremia (especially older adults), and discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly.
patient_summary: Fetzima is a once-daily antidepressant for MDD. You swallow the capsule whole (don’t crush or open it). Early changes can show up in 1–2 weeks, but real depression relief usually builds over 4–6 weeks. Common issues: nausea, sweating, constipation, sexual side effects, and sometimes higher blood pressure or a faster heart rate. It carries the standard antidepressant warning about increased suicidal thoughts/behavior in people 24 and under. Don’t mix it with MAOIs, and don’t stop suddenly—taper if you’ve been on it for a few weeks or longer.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-labeled for major depressive disorder. Early effects may show up in 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4–6 weeks.

Not a separate FDA indication in the supplied notes, but in real-world depression, anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and panic symptoms can ride along. If those symptoms intensify after starting or changing the dose, reassess quickly for activation, akathisia, bipolar spectrum illness, or emerging suicidality.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to levomilnacipran, milnacipran, or any component of the formulation
Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) intended to treat psychiatric disorders (concurrently or within 7 days of discontinuing levomilnacipran, or within 14 days of discontinuing the MAOI)
Initiation of levomilnacipran in a patient receiving IV methylene blue

efficacy_response.patient_text: With this medication, early changes can show up within 1–2 weeks, but the bigger depression shift usually builds over 4–6 weeks. If you feel worse, more agitated, more impulsive, or more suicidal at any point—especially early on or after a dose change—that’s not a “push through it” moment. That’s a call-your-prescriber moment.

pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: initial effects may be observed within 1 to 2 weeks; continued improvements through 4 to 6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be administered with or without food
pharmacokinetics.special_notes: Ethanol may accelerate drug release by interacting with extended-release properties; avoid ethanol.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Fetzima is used to treat {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder (MDD)}. This is a daily, extended-release SNRI—meaning it’s designed to give steady coverage across the day, not a quick “as needed” effect. You may notice early shifts (energy, motivation, focus) within 1–2 weeks, but the fuller depression response usually takes 4–6 weeks.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Depressed mood, low motivation, low energy, impaired focus, and loss of interest that persist and impact daily function

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Here’s what patients commonly describe—real-life, not brochure-life. Everyone’s different, but patterns show up:

quotes: I wasn’t suddenly happy, but I was less stuck. Like I could actually start things.
My brain felt a little more “online.” Still depressed, just not glued to the couch.
I had more energy—but it came with jittery edges at first.
items.note: If activation turns into agitation, insomnia, panic-y energy, or impulsivity, that can be a red flag—especially early on or after a dose change.

items.category: GI stuff (nausea is the classic one)
quotes: The nausea was loud the first week, then it chilled out.
I had that sour-stomach feeling after my dose for a while.
Eating a little something helped, even though it says food doesn’t matter.
items.note: Nausea is very common. If you can’t keep food down, that’s not normal-adjustment; that’s a message to your prescriber.

quotes: I sweat more—like, weirdly more—especially at night.
I felt flushed and clammy sometimes, even when I wasn’t anxious.
My body ran warmer than usual.
Everything worked, but the finish line took forever.
My libido dipped and it wasn’t subtle.
It helped my mood but messed with orgasms.
items.note: Sexual dysfunction can happen with SNRIs. It’s real, it’s common, and it’s worth addressing—not suffering in silence.

quotes: I could feel my heart thump more when I climbed stairs.
My pulse was higher than usual for a while.
I didn’t “feel” anything, but my blood pressure readings went up.
items.note: This medication can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Monitoring isn’t optional—especially if you already have hypertension, arrhythmias, or heart disease.

quotes: I missed a couple days and felt like my brain got zapped.
I got dizzy, nauseous, and irritable out of nowhere.
It felt like the flu plus anxiety—until I restarted and tapered properly.
items.note: Discontinuation symptoms are more likely with abrupt stops, longer treatment duration, and higher doses. Tapering matters.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Fetzima isn’t a same-day mood flip. It’s a steady build.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Early effects may start to show (often energy, drive, concentration before mood fully lifts)
4–6 weeks: Continued improvements typically accumulate across this window
6–8 hours: Time to peak concentration after a dose
Once daily: Extended-release design supports daily dosing at about the same time each day

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.value: Early effects may be observed within 1–2 weeks
sections.text: With antidepressants, the biggest trap is expecting a dramatic overnight change. With Fetzima, early shifts can show up within 1–2 weeks, but meaningful depression improvement typically keeps building through 4–6 weeks. If you’re getting worse—more agitated, more impulsive, more suicidal—especially early on or around dose changes, that’s a safety signal and needs immediate clinical attention.
sections.clinical_details: The supplied notes describe a typical antidepressant time course: initial effects may be seen within 1 to 2 weeks with continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks. Specific response/remission percentages or trial outcomes were not provided in the supplied notes.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warning: antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts/behavior in people 24 and under—especially early on and during dose changes.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. These studies did not show an increase in the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior with antidepressant use in patients older than 24 years; there was a reduction in risk with antidepressant use in patients 65 years and older.
other: Monitor closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes—particularly during the first few months or when the dose is increased or decreased
Levomilnacipran is not approved for use in pediatric patients
Serotonin syndrome can be life-threatening, especially when combined with other serotonergic agents or MAOIs
May increase blood pressure and heart rate; assess before starting and periodically thereafter
Bleeding risk may increase (impaired platelet aggregation), especially with NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin, or other anticoagulants
May cause urinary hesitancy or urinary retention; report difficulty urinating
May cause pupillary dilation and can trigger narrow-angle glaucoma in susceptible patients
May precipitate mania/hypomania in patients with bipolar disorder; screen for bipolar disorder before treating depression
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk (older adults, diuretics, volume depletion increase risk); monitor sodium when starting or changing dose in at-risk patients
Discontinuation syndrome can occur with abrupt stop or interruption—taper when stopping after sustained use
Seizures have been reported; use caution in seizure disorders
Ethanol may accelerate drug release from the extended-release capsule; avoid ethanol
patient_counseling: If you’re 24 or under (or caring for someone who is), take the suicidality warning seriously: watch for worsening depression, new agitation, insomnia, impulsivity, panic, irritability, hostility, or sudden mood shifts—especially early on or after dose changes.
Families/caregivers: close observation and fast communication with the prescriber isn’t “being dramatic.” It’s how we catch risk early.
Do not combine with MAOIs. The washout timing matters.
Know serotonin syndrome signs: agitation, confusion, sweating, fast heart rate, tremor/rigidity, diarrhea, fever—seek urgent care if these show up.
Check blood pressure and pulse. If you develop sustained hypertension or tachycardia, your prescriber may reduce the dose or taper off.
Report trouble urinating, eye pain/vision changes, severe dizziness/fainting, or severe worsening anxiety/agitation.
Don’t stop suddenly. If you need to come off, taper—your nervous system will thank you.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues are nausea, sweating, constipation, sexual dysfunction, and cardiovascular effects (blood pressure/heart rate changes). Some side effects are dose-related and may improve with time, but safety symptoms (serotonin syndrome, severe BP elevation, urinary retention, mania, suicidality) require immediate attention.
plain_language_list: Sexual side effects (libido changes, orgasm delay/absence, erectile dysfunction, ejaculatory issues)
Blood pressure or heart rate increases

common.patient_note: This is one of the most common early side effects. If nausea is mild, it often settles. If it’s severe (can’t eat, can’t hydrate, vomiting repeatedly), reach out—don’t just white-knuckle it.
Lightheadedness when standing can happen. Hydration helps, but persistent dizziness, fainting, or falls need evaluation—especially if you’re also noticing heart rate or blood pressure changes.
Sweating can be annoying and surprisingly intense. If sweating comes with confusion, fever, tremor, or diarrhea, think serotonin syndrome and seek urgent care.
Constipation is common with SNRIs. If you’re going days without a bowel movement or you have severe abdominal pain, don’t ignore it.
A faster heart rate can occur. This is one reason blood pressure and pulse checks are part of routine monitoring.
Feeling your heartbeat more strongly can happen. If you have chest pain, fainting, or a known arrhythmia, take this seriously and get evaluated.
Even small sustained increases matter over time. If your readings stay elevated, your prescriber may adjust the dose or switch medications.
If vomiting is persistent, that can spiral into dehydration and dizziness. Contact your prescriber.
If it’s harder to start peeing, or you feel like you can’t fully empty your bladder, tell your clinician. If you can’t urinate at all, that’s urgent.
Sexual side effects can affect desire, arousal, and orgasm. They’re treatable, adjustable, and discussable—bring it up.

serious: Suicidal ideation or suicidal tendencies: frequency not defined; risk is emphasized in the boxed warning for people 24 and under and during early treatment or dose changes

Serotonin syndrome: potentially life-threatening; more likely with other serotonergic agents or MAOIs; symptoms can include agitation, hallucinations/delirium, autonomic instability, tremor/rigidity/myoclonus, GI symptoms, and seizures
Severe hypertension, sustained tachycardia, or syncope: requires evaluation and possible dose reduction or discontinuation
Mania/hypomania activation in vulnerable patients (bipolar spectrum risk)
Hyponatremia/SIADH (rare but potentially severe): confusion, headache, weakness, seizures—higher risk in older adults and those on diuretics

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: With Fetzima, the biggest interaction themes are: MAOIs (absolute no), serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic meds, bleeding risk with blood thinners/NSAIDs, and alcohol concerns with the extended-release capsule.

items.with: MAOIs (psychiatric MAOIs) and IV methylene blue
items.risk: Contraindicated due to high risk of serious reactions including serotonin syndrome.
items.action: Switching rules: wait 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting levomilnacipran. Wait 7 days after stopping levomilnacipran before starting an MAOI. Do not initiate levomilnacipran in a patient receiving IV methylene blue.

items.with: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, TCAs, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, meperidine, methadone, buspirone, amphetamines, St. John’s wort, tryptophan)
items.action: Avoid unnecessary stacking. If combination is clinically required, monitor closely and educate on serotonin syndrome symptoms. Stop the medication(s) and seek urgent care if symptoms emerge.

items.with: NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin, and other anticoagulants/antiplatelets
items.risk: Increased bleeding risk (from minor bruising/nosebleeds to serious bleeding).
items.action: Use caution and monitor for unusual bruising, GI bleeding, or prolonged bleeding. Coordinate with the prescriber managing anticoagulation.

items.risk: Ethanol may accelerate drug release by interacting with extended-release properties.
items.action: Avoid ethanol while taking this medication, especially around dosing.

items.risk: Manufacturer labeling treats this as a contraindication due to serotonin syndrome concern; newer evidence in the supplied notes suggests the combination is unlikely to cause serotonin syndrome but risk is not zero.
items.action: If linezolid is necessary, coadministration may be possible with close monitoring and patient education for serotonin toxicity.

items.risk: Clinically meaningful drug interactions may exist and can require dose/frequency adjustment or avoidance.
items.action: Run a full interaction check for the entire medication list, including OTCs and supplements, before starting or adjusting the dose.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been on Fetzima for a few weeks or longer, don’t stop abruptly. Tapering helps minimize withdrawal symptoms and gives you a chance to catch relapse early.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over 2 to 4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and detect returning depression
If treatment lasted 2 to 3 weeks: taper over 1 to 2 weeks may be reasonable
If treatment lasted <2 weeks: taper is often not necessary (but individual sensitivity varies)
Go slower (around 4 weeks or more) if you’ve had withdrawal symptoms before or you’re on higher doses
If withdrawal becomes intolerable: return to the prior dose and taper more gradually
Some patients on long-term treatment (>6 months), especially those with a history of discontinuation syndrome, may do best with very slow tapers (>3 months)

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Fetzima is taken once daily as an extended-release capsule. The standard start is 20 mg daily for 2 days, then 40 mg daily. Dose increases are made in steps, based on response and side effects. Kidney function matters for the maximum dose.

adult.mdd_initial: 20 mg PO once daily for 2 days; then increase to 40 mg PO once daily
adult.mdd_titration: If needed, increase in increments of 40 mg at intervals of 2 or more days

sections.simple_explanation: This is a once-daily extended-release capsule. You swallow it whole (don’t open, chew, or crush). Dose increases are typically stepwise and based on both symptom improvement and tolerability.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Depression treatment during pregnancy and postpartum is a risk-benefit decision. This medication also has specific kidney-based maximum doses. It is not approved for pediatric patients, and older adults need extra monitoring for hyponatremia/SIADH risk.
sections.pregnancy: SNRIs are not described as first-line before conception for treatment-naive patients in the supplied notes, but patients who are effectively treated may continue their current medication when planning pregnancy unless contraindications exist. Evidence quality for some risks is low, but SNRI exposure has been associated with possible increased risk of preeclampsia and spontaneous abortion. Third-trimester exposure can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (often resolves within 2 weeks) and rare persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; dose reduction or discontinuation prior to delivery is not recommended solely to reduce neonatal adaptation syndrome risk. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible, monitor symptoms monthly with a validated tool during pregnancy, and use shared decision-making.
sections.lactation: It is not known if levomilnacipran is present in breast milk. If used while breastfeeding, monitor the infant for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain. The decision should balance infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and maternal treatment benefits.
sections.pediatrics: Not FDA-approved for pediatric patients. The boxed warning highlights increased risk of suicidal thoughts/behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing, but use with caution. Beers Criteria flags SNRIs (including levomilnacipran) as potentially inappropriate to use with caution in adults ≥65 due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk. Monitor sodium closely when initiating or adjusting the dose, especially with diuretics, low intake, or volume depletion.
sections.hepatic: No dosage adjustment necessary (adult liver impairment guidance in supplied notes).
sections.renal: Dose limits by kidney function (CrCl): ≥60 mL/minute: no adjustment necessary. 30 to 59 mL/minute: maximum 80 mg once daily. 15 to 29 mL/minute: maximum 40 mg once daily. End-stage renal disease (ESRD): use is not recommended.
sections.bariatric_surgery: Extended-release capsule: some institutions have protocols that may conflict with standard recommendations. No immediate-release formulation is available. Consider switching to milnacipran if absorption concerns arise.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and clinical worsening: monitor closely in all ages when starting therapy and during dose changes; pay extra attention in people 24 and under

Mood activation: watch for agitation, irritability, panic attacks, insomnia, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania—especially early or after dose adjustments; reassess for bipolar disorder if activation occurs
Blood pressure and heart rate: evaluate prior to initiation and periodically thereafter; consider dose reduction or gradual discontinuation for sustained hypertension or tachycardia
Serotonin syndrome surveillance when combined with other serotonergic agents: mental status changes, autonomic instability, neuromuscular signs, GI symptoms, seizures
Serum sodium in at-risk populations (older adults, diuretic use, volume depletion) and when initiating or adjusting dose
Renal function for dosing limits (maximum dose depends on CrCl; ESRD use not recommended)
Urinary hesitancy/retention: ask directly about urinary symptoms; urgent evaluation if inability to urinate
Sexual function: assess baseline and follow-up (libido, arousal, orgasm, erectile/ejaculatory function)
Eye risk: consider intraocular pressure monitoring in patients with elevated baseline IOP or narrow-angle glaucoma risk; educate about acute angle-closure symptoms
Bleeding risk: monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding—especially with NSAIDs/anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Discontinuation symptoms if doses are missed or the medication is stopped: dizziness, GI symptoms, irritability, sleep disturbances, “electric shock” sensations, mood lability—adjust taper if needed

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Fetzima is only available as an extended-release capsule. It’s designed for once-daily dosing.
items: Extended-Release Capsule (24 hour), Oral: 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg
Extended-Release Capsule Therapy Pack (Fetzima Titration): 20 mg & 40 mg (28-count pack)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Levomilnacipran is a serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI). In plain terms: it increases levels of serotonin and norepinephrine signaling in the brain by blocking their reuptake, which can improve depressive symptoms over time.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Fetzima is a once-daily SNRI option for major depressive disorder. In practice, it can be considered when depression symptoms include low energy, low drive, and impaired focus—while staying mindful that SNRIs can raise blood pressure/heart rate and can cause discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly. It is not approved for pediatric use, and patients should be screened for bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant to reduce the risk of antidepressant-induced mania/hypomania.

seo.title: Levomilnacipran (Fetzima): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Safe Tapering
seo.description: Fetzima (levomilnacipran) for major depressive disorder: once-daily dosing, what to expect in weeks 1–6, common side effects (nausea, sweating, sexual dysfunction), key warnings (suicidality, serotonin syndrome), interactions, kidney-based max doses, and how to taper safely.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Fetzima (levomilnacipran) is used to treat major depressive disorder (MDD). It’s a once-daily SNRI antidepressant in an extended-release capsule.
Take it by mouth once daily at about the same time each day, with or without food. Swallow the capsule whole—don’t open it, chew it, or crush it.

faqs.q: How long does Fetzima take to work?
faqs.a: Early effects may show up within 1–2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4–6 weeks. If you feel worse, more agitated, more impulsive, or more suicidal—especially early on or after dose changes—contact your prescriber right away.

faqs.q: What’s the usual starting dose for Fetzima?
faqs.a: Standard adult dosing starts at 20 mg once daily for 2 days, then increases to 40 mg once daily. If needed, it may be increased in 40 mg steps at intervals of 2 or more days. Maintenance is typically 40 to 120 mg once daily, with a maximum of 120 mg/day—unless kidney function limits the maximum.

faqs.q: Does kidney disease change the maximum dose?
faqs.a: Yes. If CrCl is 30–59 mL/minute, the maximum is 80 mg once daily. If CrCl is 15–29 mL/minute, the maximum is 40 mg once daily. In end-stage renal disease (ESRD), use is not recommended.

faqs.q: Can Fetzima raise blood pressure or heart rate?
faqs.a: Yes. It may increase blood pressure and heart rate. Blood pressure and pulse should be checked before starting and periodically afterward, and sustained hypertension or tachycardia may require dose reduction or gradual discontinuation.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: In the supplied notes, the most prominent listed common effects include nausea, sweating, constipation, sexual dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension/lightheadedness, and cardiovascular effects like tachycardia, palpitations, or hypertension.

faqs.q: Can Fetzima cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: Yes. Sexual dysfunction has been reported with levomilnacipran. In males this can include erectile dysfunction and ejaculatory issues; libido changes and orgasm problems can occur in any gender. If this happens, talk to your prescriber—there are options.

faqs.q: What’s the suicidality warning with antidepressants?
faqs.a: Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults (18–24) in short-term studies. The studies did not show increased risk in adults over 24, and risk was reduced in adults 65 and older. Everyone starting an antidepressant should be monitored closely for worsening depression, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes—especially early on or during dose adjustments.

faqs.q: Can I take Fetzima with an MAOI?
faqs.a: No. You need washout time. Wait 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting Fetzima. After stopping Fetzima, wait 7 days before starting an MAOI. Starting Fetzima in a patient receiving IV methylene blue is also contraindicated.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with Fetzima?
faqs.a: The supplied notes advise avoiding ethanol because alcohol may accelerate drug release by interacting with the extended-release properties. Bottom line: avoid alcohol with this medication.

faqs.q: How do I stop Fetzima without feeling awful?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for 4 weeks or more, taper gradually over about 2–4 weeks to minimize discontinuation symptoms and to catch returning depression early. For 2–3 weeks of treatment, taper over 1–2 weeks may be used. If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable, return to the prior dose and taper more slowly. Some people on long-term treatment may need very slow tapers over months.

faqs.q: Is Fetzima approved for kids or teens?
faqs.a: No. Levomilnacipran is not approved for pediatric patients.

It can. Antidepressants may precipitate mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. That’s why clinicians screen for bipolar symptoms before starting an antidepressant and monitor closely for activation symptoms after starting or changing the dose.
